t: Download trends, small enough for a footer
d: Install package-trends and draw a package's npm downloads as a sparkline, a line of text or a KPI block — no dependencies, no stylesheet, no chart library.
x: A package's npm downloads as a sparkline, a line of text or a KPI block. No dependencies, no stylesheet, no chart library — 8.3 kB for the core and 6.8 kB for the React entry, gzipped as a bundler ships them. Install npm install package-trends Three shapes, one component Sparkline Shape only, for a nav or a table cell. Text One line, inside a sentence. KPI The number leads, the chart confirms. The npm API needs no key It sends access-control-allow-origin: , so this works straight from a browser with no proxy of your own. Every chart on this site was fetched by your browser as you loaded it — change the package in the header and watch them all follow. Questions Does it need an API key or a proxy? No. The npm downloads API is public and sends access-control-allow-origin: , so a browser can call it directly. How big is it? 8.3 kB gzipped for the framework-agnostic core, 6.8 kB for the React entry, 6.9 kB for the comparison chart and 3.6 kB for the heatmap. Each figure is that entry on its own, minified and gzipped, measured on every build. There are no dependencies, and react is a peer you already have. Does it work without React? Yes. sparklineSvg returns an SVG string and the core has no framework in it. This site uses that path and loads no framework at all.

d: The default variant: shape only, no axes and no labels, sized for a nav, a list row or a table cell.
x: package-trends · Variants The default. Shape only — no axes, no labels, nothing but the line — for a nav, a list row or a table cell. <PackageTrend package="react" width={210} height={44} dot /

d: The text variant: the count, the word and the change on one line, inheriting the colour of the sentence it sits in.
x: package-trends · Variants One line: the count, the word, the change. It sets no colour of its own unless you ask, so it reads as part of the sentence around it. <PackageTrend package="react" variant="text" colors={{ up: "15803d", down: "b3261e" }} / Unset, the change inherits the surrounding colour — which is what keeps the component out of a host's palette. The data-direction attribute is on the element either way, so a stylesheet can colour it instead of a prop.

d: The KPI variant: a tile where the number leads, the change qualifies it and a small chart shows the number is not a fluke.
x: package-trends · Variants A tile. The number leads, the change qualifies it, and the chart is there to show the number is not a fluke. <PackageTrend package="react" variant="kpi" height={40} fill="color-mix(in oklab, currentColor 10%, transparent)" /

d: How the line joins its points: linear, step, or monotone cubic smoothing that can never draw a count that never happened.
x: package-trends · Charts How the line joins its points. smooth is monotone cubic, not a cardinal spline: between any two points it stays within their values, so it can never draw a count that never happened. <PackageTrend package="react" curve="linear" / Why not a cardinal spline A cardinal spline overshoots a local extreme to keep its curvature smooth. On a download count that means drawing a dip below the real low — and near zero, below zero. A reader cannot tell an invented value from a real one, so the curve has to be one that cannot invent them. Questions Why is smoothing monotone cubic rather than a spline? A cardinal spline overshoots local extremes, which on a download count draws values that never happened — below the real low, and near zero, below zero. Monotone cubic stays within the two points it joins.

d: Discrete days as columns anchored at zero, with weekly or monthly bucketing for packages busy enough that thirty bars look identical.
x: package-trends · Charts Discrete days rather than a continuous line. Columns are anchored at zero, which is the honest baseline for a count. <PackageTrend package="react" chart="column" / Thirty days of a busy package, anchored at zero, draws thirty nearly identical bars. aggregate="week" gives four or five that actually differ — columns want fewer, fatter bars than a line does.

d: Each bucket's low, mean and high drawn as a range — the honest alternative to a candlestick, which a daily count cannot fill.
x: package-trends · Charts Each bucket's low, mean and high, drawn as a range with the mean marked. <PackageTrend package="react" chart="band" bandSize={7} / Why not candlesticks A candlestick needs an open and a close — a price at the start of the period and a price at the end. A day's downloads is one number. Borrowing the shape would mean inventing two of its four values, so the band shows what the data has: the spread, and the middle.

d: Calling out the last point, the peak or the trough, and when a rule at zero is worth drawing at all.
x: package-trends · Charts Points worth calling out, and a rule at zero where zero is inside the range. <PackageTrend package="react" mark={["last", "peak"]} / axis only shows for data that crosses zero, which downloads never do — against domain="auto" the rule lands on the bottom edge and is invisible. It is there for a derived series, such as a day-over-day change, where zero sits in the middle.

d: Sizing a chart in pixels, in em so it scales with the text it sits in, or fluid so it fills its container.
x: package-trends · Scale A number is pixels. A CSS length leaves the viewBox alone and renders at that size instead, so a chart set in em scales with the text it sits in. <PackageTrend package="react" width="8em" height="1.6em" / A chart never grows past its container either way: one wider than its box scales down with its aspect ratio kept, so it cannot give the page a horizontal scrollbar.

d: The y-range values are laid out across, and why two charts side by side are only comparable on a fixed one.
x: package-trends · Scale The y-range the values are laid out across. auto runs from the series' own low to its own high — the sparkline convention. A fixed pair is the only way two charts side by side can be compared. <PackageTrend package="react" domain="auto" / Without a fixed domain a package with a thousand downloads draws exactly the same picture as one with a million. That is fine alone and misleading in a row.

d: Named periods and explicit date ranges, weekly and monthly bucketing, and why smoothing never touches the figures beside the chart.
x: package-trends · Data A named period, or an explicit pair of dates. Long periods bucket into whole weeks or months, measured back from the latest day. import { between } from "package-trends"; <PackageTrend package="react" period="last-month" / <PackageTrend package="react" period={between("2026-06-01", "2026-08-31")} / Smoothing never touches the numbers Daily counts swing threefold across the week, so the drawn line is a 7-day mean by default. Every figure beside it — total, average, peak, change — comes from the raw series, so a smoothed chart cannot quietly restate the total. Never sum trend.values: it is the drawing, not the data. Questions Can I sum trend.values to get the total? No. values is the smoothed series that gets drawn. Every figure — total, mean, peak, change — comes from the raw points, and trend.total is the one to use.

d: npm answers 0 for a day it has not aggregated, indistinguishable from a real zero. What that does to the figures, and the repair.
x: package-trends · Data npm answers 0 for a day it has not aggregated, and gives you no way to tell that from a day nobody installed the package. Taken literally those zeros are not a small error. <PackageTrend package="react" gaps="fill" / // the days npm had no data for const { gapDays } = computeTrend(await fetchDownloads("react")); Switch the policy above and watch every figure move. On a sample of react seven of thirty days came back zero: the mean fell by a quarter, the weekday profile inverted, and a flat month read as a falling one. Interior zeros are interpolated from their neighbours and listed in gapDays, so you can say so where it matters. Questions Why does npm report zero downloads for some days? Those are days the registry has not aggregated, not days nobody installed the package — and the API gives you no way to tell the two apart. package-trends interpolates interior zeros from their neighbours and lists them in gapDays.

d: Growth, linear fit and r², weekday profile, weekend ratio, volatility, spikes and streak — the figures behind a sentence about a package.
x: package-trends · Data The figures you would need to write about a package without looking at the chart. import { analyse, fetchDownloads } from "package-trends"; const a = analyse(await fetchDownloads("react", { period: "last-month" })); a.direction; // "rising" "falling" "flat" a.confidence; // "strong" "moderate" "weak", from the r² a.weekendRatio; // weekday-driven use sits near 0.6 The field to build a sentence on is confidence. A slope alone will cheerfully report that react is falling by 390,000 a day; the r² behind it is what says the month was flat and the slope is noise.

d: Several packages on one chart, on an absolute scale or indexed against their own start, and the spread figure that tells you which to use.
x: package-trends · Compare Several packages on one chart. An absolute scale only reads when the packages are of a like size — and they rarely are. import { PackageComparison } from "package-trends/compare"; <PackageComparison packages={["react", "vue", "svelte", "preact"]} scale="indexed" / On absolute react takes the top and the rest collapse onto the floor: the chart is literally true and tells you nothing. indexed restates each series against its own start, so every line begins at 100 and the chart compares growth instead of size. The spread on the comparison is what tells you which one to use.

d: Fetch once where the page is built and pass the range down, so no visitor costs a request and the chart is in the first paint.
x: package-trends · Using it Fetch once where the page is built and pass it down. No visitor costs a request, and the chart is in the first paint rather than appearing a moment later. import { fetchDownloads } from "package-trends"; import { PackageTrend } from "package-trends/react"; const data = await fetchDownloads("react", { period: "last-month" }); return <PackageTrend package="react" data={data} variant="kpi" /; Or without React at all import { fetchDownloads, computeTrend, sparklineSvg } from "package-trends"; const trend = computeTrend(await fetchDownloads("react")); const svg = sparklineSvg(trend.values, { width: 200, height: 40, dot: true }); The core is the whole library and the React entry is a wrapper over it. Every chart on this site is drawn by sparklineSvg, which is the same geometry the components use — this page loads no framework at all.

d: No stylesheet ships. The chart strokes in currentColor and sets its type in em, so it inherits a host's palette instead of imposing one.
x: package-trends · Using it Nothing ships a stylesheet. The chart strokes in currentColor and the type is set in em, so it inherits rather than imposes. / the only two colours it would choose for itself / .pt-change[data-direction="up"] { color: 15803d; } .pt-change[data-direction="down"] { color: b3261e; } The same markup on three surfaces, with nothing changed but the surrounding text colour. A component that ships its own palette fights every site it lands on.

d: Every chart carries a sentence for a screen reader, the sign always accompanies the colour, and a failed fetch renders nothing rather than breaking a footer.
x: package-trends · Using it A sparkline carries nothing a non-sighted reader can use, so every chart gets a sentence instead. <PackageTrend package="react" label="Weekly pulls from npm" / <PackageTrend package="react" label={(t) = ${t.total.toLocaleString()} downloads} / - The sentence is the SVG's <title, and label replaces it. - Red and green never carry the meaning alone — the sign is always there, which is what a reader with a colour deficiency goes by. - interactive makes the chart focusable and arrow-key navigable, and announces the day under the cursor through a live region. - A failed fetch renders nothing by default. A download count is never worth breaking a footer over.

d: The full surface: every prop on the components, every export of the core, and what each of the 4 entry points costs.
x: package-trends · Reference The full surface. 4 entry points, and your bundler drops whatever you do not import. import { … } from "package-trends"; // 8.3 kB gzipped import { … } from "package-trends/react"; // 6.8 kB import { … } from "package-trends/compare"; // 6.9 kB import { … } from "package-trends/heatmap"; // 3.6 kB Core exports Export What it does fetchDownloads(name, options) One package's range from the npm API. fetchMany(names, fetchOne) Several at once, asking for each distinct name only once. computeTrend(range, options) Totals, peak, trough and change from the raw series, plus the shaped values to draw. analyse(range, options) Growth, fit and r², weekday profile, volatility, spikes, streak. compare(ranges, options) Several ranges on one scale, absolute or indexed. sparklineSvg(values, options) A standalone SVG string, for anywhere outside React. toWeekly / toMonthly / toBands Bucketing. fillGaps / applyGaps The zero repair, on its own. formatCount / formatChange / formatExact / formatWeekday Intl-backed formatting. describeTrend(trend, locale) The sentence a screen reader gets. between(from, to) An explicit date range. Props Prop Type What it does package string The package name, scoped names included. data DownloadRange A range already fetched. When set, nothing is requested. period Period between() "last-week", "last-month", "last-year", or an explicit pair. variant "sparkline" "text" "kpi" Default sparkline. chart "line" "column" "band" The chart form. curve "linear" "smooth" "step" "step-before" How the line joins its points. domain [number, number] "auto" "zero" The y-range the values are laid out across. aggregate "week" "month" Buckets whole weeks or months back from the latest day. smooth number Moving-average window for the drawn line. Default 7. gaps "fill" "zero" What to do with the days npm has no data for. Default fill. width / height number string Pixels, or a CSS length that scales with the text. fluid boolean Fill the container's width rather than sit at a natural size. mark / markColor MarkKind[] / record Points to call out: last, peak, trough. axis / axisColor boolean / string A rule at zero where zero is inside the domain. fill / fillPattern string / FillPattern Area or bar fill, flat or patterned. stroke / strokeWidth / strokeDasharray string / number / string The line itself. colors { up, down } The rise and fall figures. Unset, they inherit. styles record Inline styles per part: weight, display, spacing. numberFormat / percentFormat Intl.NumberFormatOptions Merged over the defaults. locale string Passed to Intl. label string (trend) = string The accessible name for the chart. interactive / onActivePoint boolean / fn Pointer and keyboard inspection. fallback / renderError ReactNode / fn While loading, and when it fails. svgProps / pathProps record Anything else the elements should carry. children (state) = ReactNode Replaces the built-in markup entirely.
